R3:interp.title: Probe models for a latent fault state (Othello-style)
R3:interp.summary: Train linear or nonlinear probes on seismic foundation models such as SeisLM for stress, friction or time to failure, on lab and simulator data first and then on field data. Precedents: Othello-GPT's board state (arxiv.org/abs/2210.13382, 2309.00941), AlphaZero chess concepts, and Goodfire's Evo 2 phylogeny manifold. Inference: unlike the Othello board, crustal stress does not follow from the inputs, so the probes directly test where C2 loses the information.

R3:interp.title: Mine waveform models for new signal classes (the Evo 2 template)
R3:interp.summary: Run SAEs or manifold discovery on pretrained waveform or GPS models to catalogue the signal classes they have learned (tremor, repeating quakes, slow slip, artifacts), as Goodfire did with Evo 2 (goodfire.com/blog/interpreting-evo-2). The payoff is mostly monitoring. Candidate precursors found this way face the same single-event noise-floor problem as the GPS signal. Known SAE limits apply, including results matched by simpler baselines and curved structure being fragmented.

roots.question: Can scientific paper reviews (maybe specifically ML, DL, data-driven papers) be automated with highly scoped, small subagents following the AISLE model: many open-source models, since they have different blind spots, with tasks scoped to known failure modes like biases, factual reproduction errors, 'do these authors/papers exist' errors and overclaims, including building the suggested experiments and variations and running them on GPUs? Is compute a major blocker at some level, could a shit ton of GPU parallelism fix it?

What's actually stopping general purpose robot hands from reliably doing stuff like folding laundry or loading a dishwasher? Is it the lack of real-world manipulation data, the hardware (sensors, actuators, tactile feedback), or the sim-to-real gap? Is that a major blocker at some level, and could it be fixed by running millions of simulated robots in parallel on a shit ton of GPUs?

Why can't we predict earthquakes days or hours in advance? Is it fundamentally chaotic physics that no model can get around, or is it mostly a data problem with too few sensors and too few big quakes to learn from? Could training huge foundation models on decades of global seismic waveforms, GPS strain and fault simulations with a shit ton of GPU parallelism actually get somewhere, or is compute not the blocker at all?

What actually stops us from autoformalizing most of published math into Lean? Is it gaps in Mathlib coverage, the step of translating informal proofs where authors skip things that are 'obvious', or something deeper about how mathematicians write? The Lean kernel is a free and perfect verifier, so this looks like one of the few domains where brute-force search can't fool itself. Could you split every paper into tiny lemma-sized subgoals and throw many different open-source prover models at each one in parallel, with each model scoped to a known failure mode like wrong definitions, mismatched conventions or silently strengthened hypotheses? Is compute a major blocker at some level, and could a shit ton of GPU parallelism fix it, or is the real bottleneck checking that the formal statement means the same thing as the English one?

What limits general-purpose robot manipulation right now? Is it lack of real-world data, the sim-to-real gap, or hardware like hands and tactile sensors? If you can already run millions of simulated environments in parallel on GPUs with heavy domain randomization, why can't you brute-force a policy that folds laundry or ties knots and then transfers to a real robot? Is contact and deformable-object physics the wall that no amount of compute gets you over because the simulator itself is wrong in ways you can't randomize away? Or could a shit ton of GPU parallelism plus a small fleet of real robots that keeps correcting the simulator close the loop?

predictions.if_lever: R² left after removing signal power rises steadily from smallest to largest model in both seeds, with smallest and largest confidence intervals not overlapping.
predictions.if_not: The size curve is flat, or pretrained probes sit within the confidence interval of random-init copies or the power baseline [rouet2018].
predictions.decision_rule: Lab-state-beyond-power requires pretrained minus random-init ΔR² >= 0.05 on held-out p4679 and p4678 transfer; scaling requires monotone residual R² rise XS to L in both seeds with L and XS CIs not overlapping.
predictions.noise_rule: 95% CIs by block bootstrap over stick-slip cycles; compare sizes only when seed-to-seed spread is smaller than the gap between sizes.
predictions.expected_why: The file does not state an expected outcome; it frames a null (nothing beyond a power meter) as a useful result too.

plan.option_title: Mine waveform models for new signal classes (the Evo 2 template)
plan.question: Can sparse autoencoders on a pretrained seismic waveform model recover known signal classes and hidden events better than spectrogram clustering or single neurons?
plan.hypothesis: Sparse autoencoder features on SeisLM-large will find known signal classes and missed examples of them, beating spectrogram clustering and random-start autoencoders; a truly new class is unlikely.

compute_axis.quantity: SAE dictionary width (latents per SAE); the spike-in prevalence sweep is not a compute quantity

held_fixed: SeisLM-large released weights (12 layers, width 768, 90.7M params)
30-s windows at 100 Hz, ZNE order, per-window normalisation
Score threshold fixed on validation split, reported on test split

predictions.if_lever: Autoencoder features cost less to inspect than spectrogram clustering and single neurons, and beat the random-start autoencoder; rare classes get their own feature at 1% prevalence or below.
predictions.if_not: The pretrained autoencoder is about equal to the random-start one, or spectrogram clustering and single neurons match it; no class gets its own feature at 1% prevalence or below.
predictions.decision_rule: Stop after Stage 2 if pretrained SAE is about equal to B2 or B0/B1 match the SAE on inspection cost for most known classes; stop after Stage 3 if no class reaches best-latent F1 >= 0.5 at 1% prevalence or below.
predictions.noise_rule: 3 seeds per main SAE (2 for spike-in); a candidate latent must appear in at least 2 of 3 seeds; threshold frozen on period A and replicated on period B; blind review by two seismologists at 80% accuracy.
predictions.expected_why: The file expects known classes and missed instances of them to be recovered but a genuinely new class to be unlikely, and gives no expected outcome for the baseline comparison.

plan.compute_tested_why: The plan varies SAE width (16,384 vs 65,536) but its key test varies class prevalence (0%, 0.1%, 1%, 10%) in the training mix, which more parallel compute does not buy.
plan.scored_against: Held-out labels (F1 and AUROC), injected synthetic artifacts, spike-in recovery, hidden-event lists (445 PNW noise traces, Suarez and Beroza error list), baselines B0-B4, and SeisLM's own spliced contrastive loss versus matched-rank PCA.

arms.what: BatchTopK SAEs (plus ReLU/L1) on SeisLM-large layers 4, 8, 12
Log-spectrogram or scattering features, PCA and Gaussian-mixture clustering (B0'; band-limited energy for tremor)
Single neurons, PCA components, k-means on the same activations
Same SAE recipe on a randomly initialised SeisLM
Supervised logistic probe per label on raw activations (ceiling)
PhaseNet + EQTransformer ensemble, hidden-event test only

baseline.what: Spectrogram/scattering clustering (B0) and single-neuron/PCA/k-means (B1) inspection cost on known classes

anchor.what: SeisLM repo regression check reports exact equality between portable bundles and original checkpoints; paper's noise-vs-earthquake separation (pretrained vs random-init) reproduces on STEAD.
anchor.tolerance: exact equality for the regression check; separation qualitatively reproduces

checks: Fraction of variance explained, mean L0 and dead-latent fraction for every SAE
Spliced-loss test: replace layer output with SAE reconstruction, recompute SeisLM masked contrastive loss, compare to clean loss and to matched-rank PCA reconstruction
Synthetic artifacts (spikes, DC steps, clipping, calibration signals, zeroed segments) injected into clean noise; a dedicated latent must respond and rise with amplitude

Seven gates for a candidate new class: seed stability, not a known label (best F1 < 0.3), not metadata (AUROC < 0.7), multi-station coherence (3 or more stations), not SAE geometry artifact, blind review (>= 80%), replication in period B

phases.what: Stage 0: literature check (one hour), environment, regression and smoke tests, throughput benchmark

gate.else: Stop if the regression check fails or the noise/earthquake separation does not reproduce (spend about $34).

restructuring.sequential_part: Not a sequential chain; stages run in order but no single answer waits on a long step-by-step chain.
restructuring.condition: Only the SAE sweep parallelises; the file judges 8 GPUs not worth it. Stage 0 throughput benchmark checks actual GPU speed.
restructuring.baseline_sequential: Single H100 running all stages in sequence.

scope_gap: Slow slip is out of reach (30-s windows at 100 Hz)
Repeating earthquakes are out of scope
Pretraining mix is earthquake-heavy; rare non-earthquake signals may be weakly represented
No absolute amplitude information after per-window normalisation
A genuinely new signal class is an upside, not an expected result

records.card: **O7 · Mine waveform models for new signal classes (the Evo 2 template).** R3 · interp · random pick · compute tested: partly · plan expects: unsure · halted: cost record broken **Question.** Can sparse autoencoders on a pretrained seismic waveform model recover known signal classes and hidden events better than spectrogram clustering or single neurons? **What is known.** Goodfire's Evo 2 SAE work and InterPLM on protein models; no seismic SAE result was found, but no web search was run, so one may exist. Whether SAEs on a seismic foundation model give latents that beat spectrogram clustering, and how rare a class can be and still get its own latent. **Hypothesis.** Sparse autoencoder features on SeisLM-large will find known signal classes and missed examples of them, beating spectrogram clustering and random-start autoencoders; a truly new class is unlikely. **If compute is the lever.** Autoencoder features cost less to inspect than spectrogram clustering and single neurons, and beat the random-start autoencoder; rare classes get their own feature at 1% prevalence or below. **If not.** The pretrained autoencoder is about equal to the random-start one, or spectrogram clustering and single neurons match it; no class gets its own feature at 1% prevalence or below. **Test.** Train sparse autoencoders on three layers of SeisLM-large, score features against known labels, measure how rare a class can be and still get a feature, then scan Cascadia and Parkfield data, all on one H100 for about $700. *Compute axis.* SAE dictionary width (latents per SAE); the spike-in prevalence sweep is not a compute quantity: 16,384–65,536 latents, 2 levels. Closest prior: not on this axis. Prior art checked without web search. *Restructuring.* none. **Check first.** SeisLM repo regression check reports exact equality between portable bundles and original checkpoints; paper's noise-vs-earthquake separation (pretrained vs random-init) reproduces on STEAD. Tolerance: exact equality for the regression check; separation qualitatively reproduces. **Would not show.** No web search was run, so earlier seismic SAE work cannot be ruled out. Data-size and token-count figures are the file's inferences, not measured. Gate 6 depends on human reviewers outside the budget. *Cost.* Plans $700.66 of the $1,000 budget over 154 machine-hours, leaving $299.34. Main guess: Stage 1 instance-hours [g], measured after $228.76 of spend; the budget is reached if it is 2.9× higher.
